content: Streptomycin is prescribed for the treatment of moderate to severe infections caused by microorganisms that are susceptible to its effects. Its use is specifically indicated in the following conditions: Mycobacterium tuberculosis The Advisory Council for the Elimination of Tuberculosis, the American Thoracic Society, and the Centers for Disease Control recommend that streptomycin or ethambutol be included as a fourth drug in a treatment regimen for tuberculosis. This regimen should also include isoniazid (INH), rifampin, and pyrazinamide during the initial phase of treatment, unless the likelihood of resistance to INH or rifampin is very low. The necessity of a fourth drug should be reassessed once susceptibility testing results are available. Historically, when the national rate of primary drug resistance to isoniazid was less than 4% and either stable or declining, twoor three-drug regimens were considered sufficient. If current community rates of INH resistance remain below 4%, initial treatment regimens with fewer than four drugs may be considered. Streptomycin is also indicated for tuberculosis treatment in cases where one or more of the aforementioned drugs cannot be used due to toxicity or intolerance. The management of tuberculosis has become increasingly complex due to rising rates of drug resistance and the concurrent presence of HIV infection. In such cases, consultation with experts in tuberculosis treatment may be advisable. Non-tuberculosis Infections Streptomycin should be reserved for treating infections caused by bacteria that are proven to be susceptible to its antibacterial effects and are not treatable with less toxic agents. These infections include: Pasteurella pestis (plague) Francisella tularensis (tularemia) Brucella Calymmatobacterium granulomatis (donovanosis, granuloma inguinale) Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) Haemophilus influenzae (in respiratory, endocardial, and meningeal infections, used in combination with another antibacterial agent) Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia (used in combination with another antibacterial agent) Escherichia coli, Proteus, Aerobacter aerogenes, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterococcus faecalis in urinary tract infections Streptococcus viridans and Enterococcus faecalis in endocardial infections (used in combination with penicillin) Gram-negative bacillary bacteremia (used in combination with another antibacterial agent) To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and preserve the efficacy of streptomycin and other antibacterial drugs, streptomycin should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are confirmed or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform the empirical choice of therapy.
